\chapter{At the Doorway}
\label{ch:ta-at-the-doorway}
\hlchaptermodality{50}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the five things a guest meets at a Tamil doorway, and welcome them.}

Complete TA-C50-welcome and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[vāsal]{\ta{வாசல்} (vāsal) — a doorway}

\label{lesson:TA-C50-threshold}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: what did \emph{vāḻttu} mean, and what did \emph{mikka naṉṟi} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{வாசல்}}
\textbf{\ta{வாசல்}} (\emph{vāsal}) — \textquotedblleft{}a doorway\textquotedblright{}.

Tamil separates the opening from the thing that shuts it. \emph{kadavu}, which you have, is the door itself — the plank on its hinges. \emph{vāsal} is the doorway: the gap, the step, and the strip of ground in front of it.

Almost everything that happens when a guest arrives happens at the \emph{vāsal} rather than inside it, which is why the word carries more than architecture.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five things a guest meets at a Tamil door.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vāsal}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{kadavu}, then \emph{vāsal}, so the door and its opening sit together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{வாசல்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a doorway\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kōlam]{\ta{கோலம்} (kōlam) — the design at a doorway}

\label{lesson:TA-C50-kolam}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{vāsal} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{கோலம்}}
\textbf{\ta{கோலம்}} (\emph{kōlam}) — \textquotedblleft{}the design at a doorway\textquotedblright{}.

Rice flour, drawn freehand on the ground each morning, usually by the woman of the house and usually before the sun is up. It is decoration and welcome at once — and because the flour feeds ants and birds, it is a small daily gift to whatever comes past.

The older sense of the word is 'form, appearance, the shape a thing takes'. A \emph{kōlam} is the shape the house puts on to receive the day.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two: the doorway, and what is drawn in front of it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kōlam}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{vāsal}, then \emph{kōlam}, and let the long \emph{ō} open the second
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{கோலம்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}the design at a doorway\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[malar]{\ta{மலர்} (malar) — a flower}

\label{lesson:TA-C50-flower}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kōlam} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{மலர்}}
\textbf{\ta{மலர்}} (\emph{malar}) — \textquotedblleft{}a flower\textquotedblright{}.

The everyday word is \emph{pū}, short and plain. \emph{malar} is its fuller partner, the one that goes into names and poems and careful speech.

It also says what a flower does: \emph{malar} means 'to open, to blossom'. One shape names the act and the result of it, and Tamil saw no reason to invent a second word for the second thing.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three, and the third one arrives in somebody's hand.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{malar}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{kōlam}, then \emph{malar}, and hear the soft \emph{r} close the second
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{மலர்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a flower\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[veṟṟilai]{\ta{வெற்றிலை} (veṟṟilai) — betel leaf}

\label{lesson:TA-C50-betel-leaf}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{malar} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{வெற்றிலை}}
\textbf{\ta{வெற்றிலை}} (\emph{veṟṟilai}) — \textquotedblleft{}betel leaf\textquotedblright{}.

The end of the word is plain once you have the pieces: \emph{-ilai} is \emph{ilai}, 'a leaf'.

Betel leaf and areca nut, handed over together, are how a Tamil household says the visit mattered and the guest is owed something — at a wedding, at a farewell, at anything that counts. The leaf costs almost nothing and means a great deal, which is the usual arrangement for the things a culture puts at its centre.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four, and the fourth is the one you are sent home with.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{veṟṟilai}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{malar}, then \emph{veṟṟilai}, and let the hard \emph{ṟ} double in the second
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{வெற்றிலை} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}betel leaf\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[varavēṟpu]{\ta{வரவேற்பு} (varavēṟpu) — a welcome}

\label{lesson:TA-C50-welcome}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{veṟṟilai} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{வரவேற்பு}}
\textbf{\ta{வரவேற்பு}} (\emph{varavēṟpu}) — \textquotedblleft{}a welcome\textquotedblright{}.

Two pieces you can almost hear coming apart. \emph{vara} is the coming, from \emph{vā}, the word for 'come' you already have; \emph{ēṟpu} is the accepting, from \emph{ēṟṟu}, 'to receive'. A welcome, in Tamil, is the acceptance of somebody's arrival, and the word says that and nothing more.

\emph{varavēṟkiṟēṉ} is \textquotedblleft{}I welcome you\textquotedblright{}. At the \emph{vāsal}, over the \emph{kōlam}, with a \emph{malar} and a \emph{veṟṟilai} in hand, it is the last thing left to say at a door — and it sets you back down exactly where this book began, at a door, with \emph{vaṇakkam}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
That closes the run: a doorway, a design, a flower, a leaf, and the word for taking somebody in.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{varavēṟpu}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order — \emph{vāsal}, \emph{kōlam}, \emph{malar}, \emph{veṟṟilai}, \emph{varavēṟpu}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{வரவேற்பு} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a welcome\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
